svg.aria-label: An NTP exchange with four real timestamps, t1 to t4, and the formulas for network delay and clock offset

g.text: delay = (t4 − t1) − (t3 − t2) = 51.66 − 0.01 = 51.65 ms on the network
offset = ((t2 − t1) + (t3 − t4)) / 2 = (93.64 + 41.99) / 2 = +67.81 ms: the MacBook is behind

ol.li: The MacBook notes the time by its own clock, t1, and sends a 48-byte request. (All times are seconds past 16:55, from this chapter’s lab.)
The server notes when the request arrived, t2, and when its reply leaves, t3, by its own clock. They’re nine microseconds apart.
The MacBook notes when the reply arrives, t4. Look: by the MacBook’s clock, the reply arrived before the server sent it! That’s because the two clocks disagree.

Four timestamps are enough to separate the two unknowns. The time spent travelling is the whole round trip, minus the server’s thinking time. And if the journey took as long each way, the difference between the clocks is the average of the two “gaps”. Bob’s MacBook is about 68 milliseconds slow.

figure.figcaption: How NTP measures a clock it can’t see, across a network it can’t measure.
